clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in SIK1, which encodes salt-inducible kinase 1, a serine/threonine kinase that regulates gene transcription, including activity-dependent programmes important for neuronal function
Presents as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, with reported onsets ranging from the neonatal period through early infancy
The phenotype includes early myoclonic encephalopathy, Ohtahara-like presentations, and epileptic spasms in some children, reflecting a severe early epileptic picture
Seizures are frequently drug-resistant and accompanied by an abnormal, often discontinuous or suppression-burst, electroencephalogram in early cases
Development is typically markedly impaired, with hypotonia, poor visual and social responsiveness, and limited motor progress

The kinase acts downstream of neuronal activity, so disease reflects disrupted signal-dependent transcription rather than a direct ion-channel defect, and broad-spectrum antiseizure agents are generally used
SIK1 should be considered among the genetic causes of early infantile epileptic encephalopathy on gene-panel or exome testing
reference.pathophysiology: SIK1 encodes salt-inducible kinase 1, a member of the AMP-activated protein kinase family that phosphorylates regulators of gene transcription, including CREB-regulated transcriptional coactivators. In neurons this kinase links electrical activity to activity-dependent gene expression that supports synaptic function and development. Pathogenic variants disturb this signalling, altering the transcriptional response to neuronal activity and impairing normal circuit maturation. The resulting dysfunction produces both the severe early epilepsy and the profound developmental impairment, with the mechanism residing in disrupted intracellular signalling rather than direct membrane excitability changes.
additionalDifferentials: Early myoclonic encephalopathy of metabolic cause
Ohtahara syndrome from structural or other genetic causes
SCN2A and SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the SIK1 variant
Electroencephalography to detect suppression-burst, hypsarrhythmia, or other patterns
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable early myoclonic encephalopathy mimics
Trial of vitamin-responsive treatments while awaiting genetic results
redFlags: Suppression-burst electroencephalography with refractory neonatal seizures
Evolution to epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia
Developmental arrest with poor visual and social engagement
reference.prognosis: Most affected children have severe developmental impairment with drug-resistant epilepsy, although seizure frequency and the electroencephalographic picture may evolve over time.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because it is a kinase rather than a channel gene
Not trialling vitamin-responsive therapies before genetic confirmation in early encephalopathy
Overlooking metabolic mimics of early myoclonic encephalopathy
Assuming a static picture when the electroencephalogram and seizures evolve
references: GeneReviews and OMIM resources on SIK1-related epileptic encephalopathy
ILAE resources on early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
management: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medications (such as valproate, levetiracetam, topiramate and benzodiazepines) form the mainstay, since disrupted activity-dependent transcription rather than a channel target means no lesion-specific drug exists

Empirical trial of vitamin-responsive treatments (pyridoxine, pyridoxal phosphate, folinic acid) while awaiting genetic and metabolic results to capture treatable early-myoclonic-encephalopathy mimics
Add-on therapy for epileptic spasms (corticotropin or corticosteroids, or vigabatrin) and consideration of the ketogenic diet in drug-resistant seizures
Supportive developmental care with physiotherapy, occupational and feeding support, and management of hypotonia and visual impairment
Rescue benzodiazepine and a status-epilepticus escalation plan for acute prolonged or clustered seizures
Serial electroencephalography and developmental review to track evolution of the suppression-burst or hypsarrhythmic pattern and guide treatment
Coordinated care through paediatric neurology and epileptology, developmental paediatrics and clinical genetics
Genetic counselling for the family once the SIK1 variant is confirmed
